> 「佛可以具足色身见不？」「不也，世尊！如来不应以具足色身见。……如来说具足色身，即非具足色身，是名具足色身。」

Section twenty applies the formula to the best case the tradition has: the fully perfected body of a buddha, complete in every major and minor mark, flawless.

Can the Tathāgata be seen by that? No. What is called a fully endowed body is not a fully endowed body, therefore it is called a fully endowed body.

## 具足 makes the test harder on purpose

Earlier sections denied that an ordinary body could reveal a buddha. This one denies it for the *perfect* body — 具足, complete, lacking nothing.

The distinction matters. It is easy to agree that an ordinary appearance is not the truth. It is much harder to agree when the appearance is maximal: every mark present, every proportion correct, the thing the tradition itself depicts as the summit of form.

If the perfected form is still not the ground, then no improvement of form will ever be. That closes the entire project of becoming impressive as a route to being real.

## 即非 and 是名, on the best case

The structure is familiar by now and its application here is exact:

- 即非: this perfect body has no permanent, independent substance. It arises from conditions and appears in dependence on them.
- 是名: therefore it is called a perfect body — a conventional designation, useful, not a ground.

The book adds a symmetry worth keeping: the ordinary body and the buddha body are the same on both levels. Conditioned in arising, empty of own-nature, different only in function. The difference between a buddha's form and yours is a difference of role, not of nature.

## 定中见佛相

The specific modern misreading the book addresses: a meditator sees a radiant figure, or light, or a perfectly formed body in concentration, and concludes that the Buddha has appeared.

The section's answer is not that the experience is fake. It is that the experience is a 相 — an appearance arising from conditions, including the conditions of one's own mind. Clear, beautiful, and still an object.

Anyone who has had such an experience knows the temptation: the wish to have it again. Which is precisely the mechanism this section is describing.

## 离相 is not blindness

The overcorrection arrives immediately: then appearances are to be ignored; look at nothing; feel nothing.

离相 is not the removal of sight. It is the removal of the authority of sight — the assumption that what appears is what is. The image can be sharp, useful, even lovable. What drops is the promotion.

The book's phrasing for the ordinary case: see it, know it as conditioned, and do not climb onto it. The word 离 refers to the climbing, not the seeing.

## The test

Take the best version of yourself. Not the aspiration — the actual best: the day you performed well, the version others see, the self you would present if asked to represent your life.

Look at it as section twenty looks at the perfected body. Complete? Then: what is it made of?

If the answer is conditions — effort, luck, health, other people's regard — then you have understood why 即非 is said even here, and why it is not an insult.
